abstract: Nek9 is a member of the understudied Nek family of dark kinases. Aberrant activation of Nek9 kinase signaling has been linked to poor keratinocyte differentiation phenotypes, and is a key driver of nevus comedonicus, a rare, localized form of acne. Nek9 also has essential scaffolding roles; during mitosis the non-catalytic C-terminal domain of Nek9 binds to Nek6 and Nek7, releasing them from an auto-inhibitory conformation, and enabling proper mitotic progression. Finally, Nek9 expression has been linked to cancer proliferation. SiRNA mediated Nek9 knock-down in a panel of cancer cell lines induces G1 cell cycle arrest and inhibits proliferation when p53 is also inactivated; cell lines with functional p53 are unaffected. Presently, no selective small molecule Nek9 chemical probes are available, though a subset of promiscuous kinase inhibitors have Nek9 activity. Recently described targeted protein degradation approaches have shown that degrader molecules based on multi-targeted kinase inhibitors may effect selective kinase degradation, despite binding to many targets. In this study we report the identification and SAR of potent degraders of the NEK9 kinase that represent attractive leads for further development. Future work is needed to optimize the selectivity of the compounds.

body:
1.
Introduction
Kinases are attractive drug targets highly amenable to small molecule inhibition and targeted protein degradation. Despite this, approximately 25% of the kinome remains unannotated in terms of both function and disease association. Never in mitosis A-related kinase 9 (Nek9) is a member of the understudied Nek family of dark kinases (
Wells et al., 2018
). Aberrant activation of Nek9 kinase signaling has been linked to poor keratinocyte differentiation phenotypes, and is a key driver of nevus comedonicus, a rare, localized form of acne (
Levinsohn et al., 2016
;
Hong et al., 2004
). Nek9 also has essential scaffolding roles; during mitosis the non-catalytic C-terminal domain of Nek9 binds to Nek6 and Nek7, releasing them from an auto-inhibitory conformation, and enabling proper mitotic progression (
Richards et al., 2009
). Finally, Nek9 expression has been linked to cancer proliferation. SiRNA mediated Nek9 knock-down in a panel of cancer cell lines induced G1 cell cycle arrest and inhibited proliferation in cells where p53 is also inactivated; cell lines with functional p53 were unaffected (
Kurioka et al., 2014
).
Presently, no selective small molecule Nek9 chemical probes are available, though a subset of promiscuous kinase inhibitors have Nek9 activity (
Wells et al., 2018
). Recently described targeted protein degradation approaches have shown that degrader molecules based on multi-targeted kinase inhibitors may effect selective kinase degradation, despite binding to many targets (
Bondeson et al., 2018
;
Olson et al., 2018
). This is a key consideration for the Nek kinase family which contains 11-members that possess high homology in their ATP-binding pockets but harbor significant diversity in their C-terminal regions, making the generation of selective inhibitors especially challenging (
Fry et al., 2012
). Furthermore, degraders may act in a sub-stoichiometric fashion, and can therefore often be used at concentrations much lower than those that would be required for effective target engagement by an inhibitor (
Lai and Crews, 2017
).
In this study we report the identification and structure-activity relationships (SAR) of potent degraders of the Nek9 kinase and characterize the proteome-wide degradation profiles and kinome-wide cellular target engagement of lead compounds. Optimization of the initial hits led to identification of molecules with improved degradation selectivity by western blot against off-targets CDK6, WEE1 and PTK2B at 100 nM, following a 4 h cell treatment. These molecules represent attractive leads for further development. Future work is needed to optimize the selectivity of the compounds, in particular at longer time points and higher concentrations.

3.
Results
As part of continued efforts to annotate the degradable kinome (
Donovan et al., 2020
), we previously reported a targeted protein degrader based on a thienopyrimidine scaffold, DB-0614, which we hypothesized would bind to multiple kinases based on the reported biochemical profile of the parental inhibitor (
Fig. 1a
). (
Sim et al., 2015
) The targets of DB-0614 were evaluated in a proteomics experiment conducted in MOLT-4 cells treated with 1 μM DB-0614 for 5 h (
Fig. 1b
, ref (
Donovan et al., 2020
).). Nek9 was the most down-regulated protein, and DB-0614 was moderately selective, with only 6 other kinases, and 2 zinc-finger proteins down-regulated by 2-fold or greater. Motivated by our interest in understudied kinases, and the use of TPD to investigate these neglected targets, in this study we sought to further characterize DB-0614 and improve its Nek9 selectivity. We validated the observed Nek9 degradation by immunoblotting. Dose response studies demonstrated that maximal Nek9 degradation occurred at 125 nM (DC
90, 4 h
) DB-0614 concentration (
Fig. 1c
–
d
). We confirmed that degradation was E3-ligase dependent by evaluating DB-0614 in CRBN
−/−
MOLT-4 cells (
Fig. 1e
).
We synthesized and tested negative control compound RSS0638, which harbors a δ-lactam in place of the glutarimide ring in thalidomide, ablating the compounds ability to bind to CRBN (
Fig. 1f
). (
Huang et al., 2018
) Complete rescue of NEK9 degradation was observed in both experiments, confirming CRBN-dependence. Finally, we performed rescue experiments where cells were pre-treated for 2 h with the proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib (1 μM) or the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924 (10 μM) to block proteasomal degradation and CRL activation respectively, followed by a 4 h treatment with DB-0614. We also pre-treated cells for 2 h with thalidomide (10 μM) or parental kinase inhibitor RSS0627 (10 μM) to block engagement of CRBN or Nek9 respectively. We observed complete rescue of NEK9 degradation under all conditions, confirming the mechanism of action of DB-0614 (
Fig. 1g
).
Having established Nek9 as a degradable kinase, we sought to improve the degradation selectivity profile of DB-0614. To do so, we first evaluated the kinome-wide cellular binding profile of DB-0614 in CRBN
−/−
MOLT4 cells using the chemoproteomic binding assay KiNativ (
Patricelli et al., 2011
) under matched experimental conditions to the global proteomics analysis in
Fig. 1a
(1 μM DB-0614 for 5 h). This experiment confirmed potent cellular target engagement of NEK9 (98% inhibition of binding,
Fig. 1h
,
SI Table 1
), which was corroborated by potent inhibition of Nek9 kinase activity by DB-0614 in an
in vitro
kinase assay (IC
50
39 nM,
Fig. 1i
). The KiNativ experiment revealed a multi-targeted profile for DB-0614, with 4 kinases displaying >90% inhibition of binding to a covalent ATP-analog, including Nek9 and degradation off-target CDK6. An additional 6 kinases had >75% inhibition, including degradation off-target Wee1, and 16 kinases showed >50% inhibition including degradation off-target CDK4. The remaining kinase degradation off-targets (AAK1, PTK2B, STK17A) were not detected in the KiNativ experiment. The relationship between % inhibition and log
2
FC is plotted in
Fig. 1j
. Although many bound targets were not degraded, all degradation off-targets also showed binding by KiNativ. These data indicated that identification of a more selective Nek9 binding scaffold may improve the degradation selectivity profile. However, few Nek9 inhibitors have been reported (
Wells et al., 2018
), and our efforts to validate the biochemical and cellular activity of putative Nek9 ligands identified through in house kinome profiling, virtual screening, and the literature failed to identify more promising scaffolds for conversion into degraders (
data not shown
).
Alteration of the linker length and composition of degraders has been shown to have a dramatic effect on degradation potency and target scope for a given scaffold/ligase pair (
Donovan et al., 2020
). Encouraged by the significantly more selective degradation profile of DB-0614 relative to its binding profile, along with the highly potent Nek9 activity, we designed and synthesized a library of CRBN recruiting thienopyrimidine degraders with PEG or carbon linkers of different lengths, as well as matched negative control molecules (
Fig. 2a
). Compounds were screened by immunoblotting for Nek9 activity at 125 nM and 10 μM at 4 and 24 h (
Fig. 2b
). Analogues DB-0625, RSS0628 and RSS0634 effected potent Nek9 degradation at 4 h.
Varying the recruited E3-ligase can also have a large effect on the potency and selectivity of degraders. We previously showed that Nek9 was preferentially degraded by the CRBN recruiting DB-0614, over the matched VHL recruiting analogue RSS0680 (
Levinsohn et al., 2016
). To evaluate if this held true over multiple time points and concentrations, and when the linker length of the compound was varied, we synthesized 2 additional VHL recruiting degraders and tested them in our screen (
Fig. 2c
–
d
). Although active compounds were identified, none of the VHL recruiting degraders had comparable potency or kinetics to the CRBN recruiting series.
We next evaluated the activity of our most potent degraders against the off-targets Wee1, PTK2B, and CDK6 at 4 h and 24 h across a range of doses (
Fig. 3a
–
b
and
SI Fig. 2
).
Although off-target degradation was observed for all compounds, RSS0634 had reduced off-target degradation at 50 nM and 100 nM compared to DB-0614 and DB-0625 at the 4 h time point (
Fig. 3a
,
Fig. S2C
). At the 24 h time point, significant off-target was observed for all compounds (
Fig. 3b
,
Fig. S2B
,
D
).
To further characterize RSS0634, we evaluated its activity against Nek9 across an expanded range of doses, observing potent Nek9 degradation at 50 nM, and maximal degradation at 1 μM RSS0634 concentration. Additionally, we saw degradation potency decrease at 10 μM, consistent with a hook effect, which is commonly observed for bifunctional molecules. We performed rescue experiments with negative control RSS0637, as well as pre-treatment of carfilzomib, MLN4924, RSS0627 and thalidomide followed by treatment with RSS0634 as described above, which confirmed the mechanism of action of RSS0634 (
Fig. 3c
–
d
).
4.
Discussion
Despite the importance of kinases as cellular signaling hubs and tractable therapeutic targets, the biological function and disease contributions of up to one quarter of the kinome remain uncharacterized. Investigating the function of understudied kinases is a major goal of the NIH Illuminating the Druggable Genome program. However, development of high-quality chemical tools for understudied kinases can be highly challenging as there are often few bioactive molecules, assays and downstream signaling pathways defined. Targeted protein degraders are valuable and highly sought research tools for interrogating the biological function of proteins, and for therapeutic target validation. These chemical tools effect degradation of the kinase of interest in endogenous systems, enabling the study of primary cellular responses, which may be transient, as well as secondary responses such as downstream signaling and adaptive or acquired resistance mechanisms.
The Nek-kinases are a subfamily of poorly understood enzymes, with 9 of the 11 family members on the NIH list of dark kinases. Through efforts to annotate the degradable kinome, we identified Nek9 as a degradable kinase (
Fry et al., 2012
). In this study, we developed multi-targeted thienopyrimidine-based degrader DB-0614 into a potent degrader with a Nek9-biased selectivity profile (RSS0634) through linker, E3-ligase and dose optimization. Importantly, this series has no Nek-family degradation off-targets, despite potent cellular binding of the parental kinase ligand to Nek1 and Nek3. RSS0634 represents an exciting new lead for further optimization into a chemical probe, and as a tool for initial investigations into Nek9 function. This approach is likely to be applicable to other dark kinases for which multi-targeted binders have been identified, particularly those that are members of closely related multi-gene subfamilies and those that have annotated leads through chemoproteomic kinase degrader profiling efforts.
